tldr: This research feeds normal force, contact area, and center of pressure (CoP) from thin pressure insoles into reinforcement learning observations, balancing impact suppression and stable support through phase-aware rewards. On a real Unitree G1 humanoid, compared to a strong perceptive baseline, it reduced peak touchdown force by up to 48.8%, reduced impact noise by up to 30.1 dB, and increased stance contact area by up to 23.8%.
hero_caption: Overall framework of TactileStep. Low-dimensional contact features obtained from a lightweight tactile simulator are fed into the policy (Actor) alongside depth and proprioception. Locomotion is divided into four phases, using two critics—a Dense Critic and a Sparse Critic—to learn rewards for impact reduction and support stabilization.
overview:
In recent years, advances in reinforcement learning and Sim-to-Real transfer have enabled humanoid robots to perform parkour maneuvers, traversing stairs and ledges. However, conventional vision-centric policies focus heavily on "whether the task is completed," often leading to heavy slamming landings or wobbling dangerously on step edges. In real-world environments, the resulting noise, mechanical wear, and fall risks cannot be ignored.

Humans naturally rely on rich tactile feedback from the soles of their feet, subconsciously modulating landing compliance and foot placement according to terrain stiffness and edges. The authors thought: "What if we define a sole tactile representation with a small Sim-to-Real gap, allowing the policy to directly observe that information and perform feedback control during touchdown and stance?"

Specifically, they built a lightweight tactile model that extracts three physical quantities from sole pressure distribution: normal force, contact area ratio, and center of pressure (CoP). Furthermore, they divided locomotion into four phases, proposing phase-aware learning that delivers appropriate rewards before touchdown, during landing, and throughout stance, along with a Dual-Critic architecture to stably learn rewards operating across different time scales.

Evaluations on a real Unitree G1 humanoid demonstrated up to a 48.8% reduction in peak touchdown impact force and up to a 30.1 dB drop in impact noise compared to a strong perceptive parkour baseline. Rather than simply stepping weakly, it expanded the stance contact area by up to 23.8%, showing that quiet, soft, and stable walking can truly be achieved.
contributions: Constructed a practical, low-dimensional tactile representation usable across simulation and real hardware by extracting normal force, contact area, and center of pressure (CoP) from sole pressure arrays.

Designed a phase-aware reward system that subdivides locomotion into four phases, promoting pre-touchdown deceleration, impact mitigation, and stance contact stabilization at physically meaningful timings.
Proposed a lightweight raycast- and diffusion-based tactile simulation running fast on rigid-body simulators, paired with a Dual-Critic architecture that decouples dense and sparse rewards.
Demonstrated substantial reductions in impact force and noise alongside expanded contact area during stair and ledge traversal using a real Unitree G1 humanoid and thin wireless pressure insoles.

sections.heading: The Next Frontier in Parkour: Not Just Traversing, but Stepping Softly and Stably
sections.summary: Humanoid locomotion control can now traverse complex terrains, but harsh landing impacts and unstable edge contacts remain significant challenges. Vision only captures terrain geometry prior to contact, and proprioception alone cannot directly perceive sole contact states. This work bridges this sensing gap by incorporating compact features from sole pressure sensors into the control loop.
sections.details:
Humanoid locomotion has advanced remarkably, achieving parkour maneuvers that cross uneven terrains and stairs impassable for wheels or tracks. However, many current learned policies prioritize "task success" above all else, often slamming down with massive impacts when jumping off high ledges or balancing unstably with only toe tips hooked on stair edges. For practical deployment alongside humans, "soft landings" that curb vibrations, noise, and actuator wear, as well as "stable support" that prevents falls, are indispensable.

Why was this difficult for existing methods? A fundamental sensing mismatch exists. Vision and elevation heightmaps from cameras or depth sensors only tell us terrain geometry *before* the foot touches down. Meanwhile, landing compliance and support stability depend on contact states established *after* touching the ground. Proprioception from joint encoders, IMUs, or estimated ground reaction force (GRF) helps to some degree, but cannot directly reveal the fine-grained load distribution across the sole. This contrasts sharply with humans, who use cutaneous sole sensations to cushion shocks and distribute loads.

Therefore, this paper proposes TactileStep, a deployable tactile learning framework utilizing pressure insoles on hardware. Because high-dimensional raw tactile images exhibit an overly large Sim-to-Real gap, they are aggregated into compact physical features: normal force, contact area ratio, and center of pressure (CoP). This enables the policy to directly modulate contact quality through closed-loop control during touchdown and stance phases.

sections.heading: Foothold Selection, Tactile Sim-to-Real, and the Path to Soft Landing
sections.summary: Conventional humanoid locomotion predominantly relied on vision-based foothold safety evaluations, yet could not regulate post-touchdown support quality. By integrating soft-landing research and tactile Sim-to-Real insights seen in quadrupeds, this work brings novel online tactile feedback to humanoid parkour across height variations.
sections.details:
### Foothold Objectives and Support Regulation
Recent vision-based humanoid locomotion has used geometric strategies to prevent hazardous steps, such as edge penalties on stairs or rewards considering sole mesh overlap with terrain. However, even if a geometrically feasible foothold is selected, the posture quickly destabilizes if sufficient contact area is not attained after landing, or if the center of pressure (CoP) shifts toward the boundary of the support polygon. While prior work noted that sole information aids balance in static postures or partial contacts, few integrated it fully into reinforcement learning for dynamic parkour locomotion.

### Tactile Simulation and Sim2Real Learning
Tactile Sim-to-Real approaches range from binary contact indicators to complex models solving deformation and shear forces. However, detailed soft-body simulation is computationally too heavy for massively parallel reinforcement learning. This work balances simulation efficiency and Sim-to-Real transferability by approximating load distribution and diffusion from rigid-body contact forces to taxels, passing only low-dimensional features (normal force, area, CoP) to the policy.

### Soft Landing in Legged Locomotion
Landing impact reduction was historically addressed with passive compliance mechanisms or local feedback, which depended heavily on mechanical hardware and complex controller tuning. Recently, learning-based studies, primarily on quadrupeds, have emerged using touchdown velocity penalties or noise constraints. For humanoids, while works like QuietWalk predicted ground reaction forces from sole sensors to apply penalties during training, they did not use online tactile feedback during real-world deployment, and were restricted to flat terrain. Deploying real-world tactile sensing for soft landings in parkour environments with significant elevation drops is a distinct differentiator.

sections.heading: The TactileStep Mechanism: Lightweight Tactile Modeling and Phase-Aware Rewards
sections.summary: The RL policy receives three features computed from sole pressure: normal force, contact area, and CoP. By building a lightweight simulator that approximates tactile array outputs from rigid-body contacts, dividing locomotion into four phases (Swing, Pre-Landing, Landing, Stance) with phase-aware rewards, and employing a Dual-Critic, effective learning is achieved.
sections.details:
The core of TactileStep lies in expressing sole contact states as "low-dimensional features directly measurable on real hardware" and feeding them directly into the control loop.

### 3.1 Problem Formulation and Policy Inputs/Outputs
The control problem is formulated as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) and optimized via PPO. In addition to proprioception (angular velocity, projected gravity, velocity commands, joint positions/velocities, and previous actions) and depth image history, the policy (Actor) receives tactile features for each foot: normalized normal force $\bar{F}$, center of pressure $\mathbf{p}^{\mathrm{cop}}$, and normalized contact area ratio $\bar{A}$ (16 dimensions across a 2-frame history). Action outputs are 29-DoF target joint positions converted to motor torques via PD control.

### 3.2 Fast Tactile Simulation and Sim-to-Real Alignment
To avoid bottlenecking massively parallel reinforcement learning, a 3-stage lightweight simulator allocates rigid-body contact forces to 60 sole taxels inside Isaac Sim.
- **Force Distribution**: Raycasts from each taxel compute ground distance $\mathrm{gap}_i$ and surface normal alignment. Contact force $F$ is distributed weighted toward taxels closer to the ground with aligned normals.
- **Spatial Diffusion**: To alleviate extreme point contacts typical of rigid simulators, loads are diffused across the $k$ nearest taxels, approximating load dispersion from sole rubber compliance.
- **Feature Extraction**: From smoothed pressure maps, contact area ratio $A$ is calculated from taxels above a threshold, CoP from a weighted average, and normal force $F$ from the total sum, followed by normalization. Using these statistics instead of raw pressure maps cushions differences in taxel layouts and calibration errors on hardware.

### 3.3 Phase-Aware Rewards and Dual-Critic
Conventional fixed-clock gait phases cannot capture subtle touchdown timings. TactileStep classifies foot states into four phases (Swing, Pre-Landing, Landing, Stance) in real time using contact force, area, foot vertical velocity, and foot height.
- **Pre-Landing**: Penalizes foot vertical velocity and acceleration, curbing harsh stomping motions into the ground.
- **Landing**: Penalizes sharp contact force spikes ($\Delta \bar{F}$) and peak forces within the landing window, softening impacts.
- **Stance**: Encourages large contact area, rewards CoP margin relative to the support polygon boundary, and penalizes rapid CoP shifts, promoting stable sole support.

Furthermore, rewards are partitioned into "Dense" signals occurring frequently each step (e.g., velocity tracking, posture maintenance) and "Sparse" signals meaningful only during specific events (e.g., peak touchdown force, phase constraints). Assigning dedicated critics to each in a Dual-Critic setup prevents value estimation interference and enables stable training.

sections.heading: Validation on Unitree G1: Dramatic Reductions of 48.8% in Force and 30.1 dB in Noise
sections.summary: Validation was performed across flat terrain, slopes, stairs, and ledges in simulation and on a real Unitree G1. TactileStep substantially lowered touchdown impact force and noise compared to perceptive baselines while enlarging stance contact area. Ablations confirmed that both tactile observations and phase-aware rewards are essential for these gains.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup and Baselines
A real Unitree G1 (29 DoF) was equipped with thin wireless pressure insoles operating at 25 Hz on each foot. Baselines included the strong perceptive parkour policy from "Hiking in the Wild" (Baseline), an ablation without tactile observations (w/o tac obs), and ablations removing specific rewards (w/o soft landing, w/o stable). Evaluation metrics included touchdown impact force $F_{\mathrm{impact}}$, stance contact area ratio $A_c$, and peak A-weighted sound pressure level $L_{A,\mathrm{peak}}$ measured by a sound level meter on the lower leg.

### 4.2 Simulation Results
Across 4,096 parallel simulation environments, TactileStep achieved the lowest landing impact force across all terrain types. The effect was particularly notable on stairs and ledges; the w/o soft landing ablation confirmed that phase-aware soft-landing rewards are critical for impact mitigation. TactileStep also surpassed the baseline and w/o stable in contact area and CoP margin, proving that the foot achieves wider and more stable ground support after landing.

### 4.3 Real-Robot Validation Results
Hardware experiments clearly mirrored the simulation trends.
- **Soft Landing (Q1)**: Compared to the baseline, touchdown impact force decreased by up to 48.8%, showing especially large gaps on discontinuous ledges. Peak landing impact noise decreased by up to 30.1 dB (robot fan background noise was ~55-60 dB). Force sensor profiles and sound meter logs consistently confirmed reduced impacts.
- **Stable Support (Q2)**: On terrains requiring steady support, contact area ratio improved by up to 23.8%. This proves the robot is not merely stepping gingerly with partial contact, but absorbing shock while firmly planting the full sole against the ground.
- **Importance of Tactile Inputs (Q3)**: In the ablation without tactile observations at deployment (w/o tac obs), despite using tactile rewards during training, improvements in noise and contact area deteriorated significantly. Online tactile observations are indispensable for perceiving and adjusting contact conditions in real time.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Humanoid Locomotion Moves from "Can It Traverse?" to "How Softly Does It Step?"
sections.summary: This study presented the sole tactile learning framework TactileStep, elevating contact interaction into a core objective of locomotion control. Using a lightweight tactile simulator and phase-aware rewards, it demonstrated on hardware that humanoids can land and support stably while suppressing impact.
sections.details: TactileStep moves humanoid terrain traversal beyond binary success/failure checks, directly optimizing the quality of foot-ground physical interaction. By utilizing hardware-accessible pressure insole features (normal force, contact area, CoP) as policy inputs and matching them with a lightweight simulation model, the Sim-to-Real gap remains minimal. Furthermore, phase-aware rewards naturally guide cautious pre-touchdown deceleration, impact cushioning at landing, and reliable load distribution during stance. As a result, humanoid robots gain a quieter, hardware-friendly, and physically refined gait suitable for shared human environments.

sections.heading: Limitations and Future Work: High-Speed Running and Sensor Durability Challenges
sections.summary: Several hurdles toward full deployment remain, including gait velocity constraints, manually designed phase detection, and reliance on rigid-body contact models. Future work will target faster motions, deformable terrains, and sensor drift mitigation.
sections.details:
The authors candidly discuss limitations and future improvements at the end of the paper:
- **Velocity Constraints**: Experiments were conducted within set velocity ranges; high-speed running or sprinting with ultra-short contact times and higher impacts has not been tested.
- **Rule-Based Phase Estimation**: Classifying the four phases relies on manually tuned thresholds for contact forces and foot velocities. End-to-end learning of latent phase representations directly from observations could enhance robustness across diverse terrains and speeds.
- **Terrain Deformability**: The simulator assumes rigid-rigid contact, offering no accuracy guarantees on deformable or granular terrains like sand, mud, or grass.
- **Sensor Durability and Drift**: Wear, drift, and recalibration demands over extended use of physical insoles remain unevaluated.
- **Failure Recovery**: Fall recovery behaviors have not been systematically analyzed, calling for further disturbance-rejection testing.

sections.heading: Appendix: Parallel Simulation Setup and Dual-Critic Training Details
sections.summary: The appendix details the massively parallel evaluation environment, ablation studies demonstrating the utility of Dual-Critic, precise definitions of Dense and Sparse rewards, and tactile noise modeling inside simulation.
sections.details:
### Parallel Simulation Evaluation Protocol
Simulation evaluations were performed across 4,096 parallel environments on a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU. Six terrain categories—flat, slope, stair ascent/descent, and ledge ascent/descent—were evaluated fairly across policies using identical cached terrain instances.

### Dual-Critic Ablation
The proposed Dual-Critic (separating Dense and Sparse value functions) was compared against a Single-Critic architecture under identical rewards and training steps. The Dual-Critic consistently maintained lower landing impact forces and higher CoP margins and contact areas. Decoupling frequent per-step signals (like posture tracking) from sparse discrete signals (like peak impact forces) effectively prevented gradient interference.

### Tactile Noise Modeling
To bolster Sim-to-Real robustness, three types of noise were injected into simulated taxel forces: force scale errors, taxel coordinate calibration offsets, and measurement latency. Furthermore, addressing the 25 Hz wireless insole update rate, comparisons against 100 Hz wired logs confirmed that 25 Hz rising-edge detection captures impact peaks with sufficient fidelity.

captions.F7: Massively parallel scene across six terrain categories (flat, slope, stair ascent/descent, ledge ascent/descent) used for simulation evaluation. Identical terrain instances ensure rigorous and fair comparisons across policies.

takeaways: Condensing sole pressure distributions into low-dimensional physical features—normal force, contact area, and CoP—dramatically reduces the Sim-to-Real gap.
Replacing fixed-clock gait cycles with a 4-phase decomposition (Swing, Pre-Landing, Landing, Stance) allows impact penalties and support rewards to be applied at precisely the right moments.
Decoupling dense and sparse rewards using separate critics in a Dual-Critic architecture stabilizes multi-objective locomotion learning in parkour tasks.
Leveraging online tactile feedback at deployment alongside vision and proprioception suppresses humanoid impact noise by over 30 dB while expanding contact support area.
limitations: Phase estimation relies on manually engineered threshold rules, which may falter under abrupt velocity changes or unfamiliar rough terrains.
Tactile simulation assumes rigid-body contact, making it difficult to directly apply to soft or deformable grounds like sand or mud.
Evaluation is still lacking regarding sensor wear, sensitivity drift, and long-term mechanical durability of the thin pressure insoles.
